title: Why greedy is correct
sub: Candy in two passes, a lower bound and the exchange argument — and where greedy breaks: coins 1, 3, 4
cards/0/title: Candy (#135): the problem and why one pass is not enough
cards/0/body:
Candy (LeetCode #135, hard). Children stand in a row, each with a rating. Everyone gets at least one candy; a child rated higher than a neighbour gets more candies than that neighbour. Find the minimum number of candies. n ≤ 2·10⁴.

Two subtleties in the statement. Equal ratings require nothing: [1, 2, 2] → 1, 2, 1 — 4 in total, the third child is fine with one. The rule is two-sided: a child is compared with both the left and the right neighbour. A left-to-right pass sees only the left one: on [3, 2, 1] it hands out 1, 1, 1 — not enough for the first two.

Naively you give everyone one candy and fix violations while any remain. On decreasing ratings each pass fixes one more position: up to n passes of O(n) — O(n²), 4·10⁸ steps for n = 2·10⁴.

The question of this lesson is wider than Candy: a greedy solution is easy to come up with and easy to get wrong. In an interview you are expected to explain why it is correct — or find a counterexample.
cards/1/q: Ratings [1, 3, 2, 2, 1]. What is the minimum number of candies?
cards/1/explain: The first two is lower than the three on its left, and on its right is an equal two — no rules apply, one candy is enough. The three is higher than both neighbours, who have one each — it gets 2. The second two is higher than the one on its right — it gets 2. Equal ratings need not get equal candies: 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7.
cards/1/wrong/1: Equal ratings require nothing — neither more nor the same. These are extra candies.
cards/1/wrong/2: That is what one left-to-right pass hands out: the second two is higher than its right neighbour but got the same amount.
cards/1/wrong/3: The three is higher than its neighbours and must get more than them.
cards/2/title: The idea: two passes and a lower bound
cards/2/body:
Pass 1, left to right: if the rating is higher than the left neighbour's, give one more than the neighbour, otherwise 1. That is the minimal distribution satisfying all the "left" rules. Pass 2, right to left: if the rating is higher than the right neighbour's, raise it to max(own, right + 1).

Why max does not break pass 1. The second pass only increases. If child i is higher than its left neighbour, raising i keeps the "more than the left one" rule. If it is lower, the left neighbour comes next in pass 2 and will rise itself if needed. Plain assignment of right + 1 is not allowed: it could lower what pass 1 gave.

Why it is the minimum — a lower bound. Say an increasing run of length L leads to i from the left (i is its L-th element). In any valid distribution, candies grow by at least one at each step of that run, so i gets at least L. From the right, likewise, at least R. So in any solution i gets at least max(L, R) — and our two passes give exactly max(L, R), and the distribution is valid. You cannot do better.

Time O(n), memory O(n). Pass 1 computes L, pass 2 computes max(L, R) in place.
cards/2/deep:
O(1) memory. There is a one-pass solution over "slopes": track the length of the current ascent up and descent down. On an ascent add up + 1, on a descent add down (the whole descent shifts up by one), and when the descent grows longer than the preceding ascent, the peak grows by one too. Equal ratings reset both counters. It is more code and easier to get wrong; in an interview you give the two passes first and mention this version as a memory improvement.

The formula as a self-check. candies[i] = max(L[i], R[i]), where L and R are the lengths of the increasing runs reaching i from the left and from the right. Working out L and R on paper for a small example is a quick way to check your code in an interview.
cards/3/explain: Pass 1 gives one more than the left neighbour. Pass 2 starts at n − 2: the last child has no right neighbour, and starting at n − 1 the code would read ratings[n] and crash. And max rather than assignment: pass 2 must not lower what pass 1 gave.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on [1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3, 2]. The rig only shows steps where a candy count changes. It stops twice during the second pass and asks what comes next.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: It stays 2: pass 1 already gave more than the left neighbour
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: 3 — the same as the right neighbour
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Pass 2 has reached i = 5: rating 5, and on the right a rating of 4 with 3 candies. After pass 1, i = 5 has 2 candies. How many will it have?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: Rating 5 is higher than the right neighbour, so it needs more candies than that neighbour: at least 3 + 1 = 4. Pass 1 gave 2 — enough only against the left neighbour. max(2, 4) = 4, and the left rule still holds: i = 4 has one candy.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: i = 3 keeps 4 = max(4, 1 + 1), and the trace goes straight to the total
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: i = 3 gets 5: one more than before
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: What is left is i = 4 (rating 2, lower than its right neighbour 5 — no rule applies) and i = 3: rating 4, higher than the 2 on its right; i = 3 has four candies, its right neighbour one. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: i = 3 already has 4 > 1 — the right rule holds, max(4, 2) = 4, and the trace does not show this step: nothing changes. Had the code assigned 1 + 1 = 2, the child rated 4 would have fewer candies than the left neighbour rated 3 with three candies. The total is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21.
cards/5/title: How to prove a greedy solution in an interview
cards/5/body:
Three ways, most common first.

1. The exchange argument. State the greedy choice precisely. Take any optimal solution O. If its first choice differs from the greedy one, swap in the greedy choice and show the solution stays valid and is no worse. So some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice; what remains is the same problem, smaller — induction.

On Non-overlapping Intervals from the second lesson: the greedy choice g is the interval with the earliest end. Let o be the first interval by end in an optimal set. end(g) ≤ end(o), and all other intervals of the set start no earlier than end(o) — hence no earlier than end(g). Replacing o with g breaks nothing, and the size is the same.

2. "Greedy stays ahead". Show that after every step the greedy solution is at least as good as any other by some measure. Jump Game: after step i, reach is the farthest cell that any path through cells 0..i can get to.

3. A lower bound. Prove that every solution is at least X and exhibit a greedy one equal to X — as in Candy.

The same exchange works in Assign Cookies (#455): the least demanding child gets the smallest cookie that satisfies them. If in an optimum they got a bigger one, swapping with whoever got the smaller suitable cookie leaves no one worse off.
cards/5/deep:
When greedy works in general. For "pick a maximum-weight subset" problems there is an exact answer: greedy by decreasing weight is optimal for every choice of weights if and only if the family of feasible subsets is a matroid. Its key property is exchange: from a larger feasible set you can always add an element to a smaller one. An example is the minimum spanning tree: Kruskal's algorithm is greedy on the graphic matroid. You need not say the word in an interview, but the exchange argument is exactly this.

Scheduling as exchange. In the proof for #435, after replacing o with g you need induction: remove g and everything that starts before end(g), and apply the same reasoning to the rest. That is precisely what the loop with the end line does.
cards/6/q: In the proof for Non-overlapping Intervals, the first interval by end o of an optimal set is replaced with g, the interval with the earliest end. Why does the set stay free of overlaps?
cards/6/options/0: g ends no later than o, and the other intervals of the set start no earlier than the end of o
cards/6/options/2: g starts before all the other intervals
cards/6/options/3: After the swap the set has fewer intervals
cards/6/explain: The other intervals of the set did not overlap o, so they start no earlier than end(o) ≥ end(g). They do not overlap g either. The size of the set is the same, so it is still optimal and now starts with the greedy choice.
cards/6/wrong/1: Length is irrelevant: greedy by length breaks on [1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10]. What matters is where the interval ends.
cards/6/wrong/2: g may well start after o. For the intervals to the right, what matters is the end of g, not its start.
cards/6/wrong/3: Swapping one for another does not change the size — that is why the set stays optimal.
cards/7/body:
Making change: reach a sum with the fewest coins. Greedy takes the largest coin that fits. For 1, 5, 10, 25 (and for the usual sets of coins and notes) this is optimal. For 1, 3, 4 and a sum of 6 it is not: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 — three coins, while 3 + 3 is two. The exchange fails here: no optimal solution starts with the four. Arbitrary denominations need DP, dp[s] = min(dp[s − c] + 1) — it is in the backtracking and DP unit.

Knapsack. Fractional — you may take part of an item — greedy by value per kilogram is optimal. 0/1 — an item whole or not at all — it is not: capacity 50, items (10 kg, 60), (20 kg, 100), (30 kg, 120). By value per kilogram you take the first two — 160, while the optimum is the second and third, 220.

How to catch it in an interview. Before coding, try to break the greedy on 2–3 elements: odd denominations, a long cheap item against a short valuable one. If it does not break, look for a proof using one of the three methods. If it breaks, that is your signal for backtracking or DP.

In games greedy is often an honest heuristic rather than an exact algorithm: packing sprites into an atlas (the exact problem is NP-hard), fitting effects into a frame budget of milliseconds (that is a knapsack). Greedy by "value per millisecond" is fine, but say out loud that it is not optimal.
cards/7/deep:
Canonical coin systems. A set of denominations on which greedy is optimal for every sum is called canonical. You do not have to check every sum: it is known that if a counterexample exists, the smallest one is less than the sum of the two largest denominations. For 1, 3, 4 that is 6 < 7 — exactly our example. So the check is DP or brute force up to that bound.

Greedy inside exact algorithms. Dijkstra is a greedy choice of the nearest vertex, and it is correct only with non-negative weights: a negative edge breaks the argument "the nearest one is already final". Same pattern: a greedy choice plus the condition under which the exchange works.
cards/8/q: Where does the greedy choice give the optimum? Select all that apply.
cards/8/options/0: Coins 1, 5, 10, 25: take the largest coin that fits
cards/8/options/1: Coins 1, 7, 10 and a sum of 14: take the largest coin that fits
cards/8/options/2: As many non-overlapping intervals as possible: take the one ending first
cards/8/options/3: 0/1 knapsack: take items by decreasing value per kilogram
cards/8/options/4: Fractional knapsack: take items by decreasing value per kilogram
cards/8/options/5: As many non-overlapping intervals as possible: take the shortest one
cards/8/explain: 1, 5, 10, 25 is a canonical set. 1, 7, 10 is not: greedy gives 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 — five coins, while 7 + 7 is two. The earliest end is proven by exchange. The fractional knapsack is exchange too: trade part of a cheap kilogram for a valuable one. The 0/1 knapsack breaks on (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120) with capacity 50, and the shortest interval breaks on [1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10].
cards/9/q: On [1, 2, 3, 4, 2] this code hands out 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 — 9 in total, but the answer is 11. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: After pass 1 the four has 4 candies. Pass 2 sees that 4 is higher than the two on its right and assigns 1 + 1 = 2 — a decrease. Now rating 4 has fewer candies than rating 3 on its left. It needs Math.Max(candies[i], candies[i + 1] + 1): pass 2 may only raise.
cards/10/q: Candy in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: do equal ratings require anything? What is n?
cards/10/items/1: Naive: fix violations while any remain — O(n²) on decreasing ratings
cards/10/items/2: The idea: a left pass fixes the left rules, a right pass with max fixes the right ones
cards/10/items/3: Why it is minimal: i gets at least the length of the increasing run from the left and from the right
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: one child, all equal, strictly decreasing ratings
cards/10/explain: For a greedy problem the "why it is minimal" step is a required part of the explanation, not a deep-dive extra: without it the interviewer cannot tell whether you guessed or understand. Strictly decreasing ratings check that pass 2 starts at n − 2 and lifts the whole chain.
cards/11/q: Match the problem with a way to prove (or refute) the greedy.
cards/11/pairs/0/1: Lower bound: runs from left and right
cards/11/pairs/1/1: Exchange: earliest end replaces the first
cards/11/pairs/5/1: Exchange: least demanding gets the smallest
